captions.instagram:
How does a microwave oven work?

A microwave oven is a radio transmitter in a metal box. Electrons whirl in a magnetron to make 12 cm waves that twist water molecules 2.45 billion times a second. Take one apart in 3D and find the hot spots.

→ A microwave oven is a metal box, a magnetron that makes the waves, and a lot of high voltage.
→ At about 4,000 volts the magnetron makes microwaves, and a metal duct pipes them into the box.
→ In a magnetron, a magnet bends electrons into spokes that whirl past ten copper cavities.
→ Weaken the magnet and the electrons crash straight into the copper: no microwaves at all.
→ Water molecules are lopsided. The microwave field flips them 2.45 billion times a second, and the jostling is heat.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/microwaveclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a microwave oven work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A microwave oven is a radio transmitter in a metal box. Electrons whirl in a magnetron to make 12 cm waves that twist water molecules 2.45 billion times a second. Take one apart in 3D and find the hot spots.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/microwaveclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/microwaveclear

In this video:
• A radio transmitter in a metal box. A transformer, a capacitor and a diode turn mains electricity into about 4,000 volts.
• Electrons whirling past copper cavities. In the magnetron, electrons boil off a hot cathode and rush towards a copper anode.
• Twisting water molecules. Water molecules have a positive end and a negative end.
• It doesn't cook from the inside out. In wet food, most of the microwave power is used up in the outer 1 to 2 cm.
• Hot spots 6 cm apart. Waves bouncing between the walls add up into a standing wave with hot and cold spots about half a wavelength, 6 cm, apart.
• Safe by design, and 50% means on and off. The door's mesh holes are about 1 to 2 mm across, far too small for a 12 cm wave to squeeze through, and interlock switches cut the power when it opens.
